name: Payment System (Stripe-like)
description: Design a payment processing system like Stripe. Covers idempotency, exactly-once processing, bank integrations, ledger accounting, and webhook notifications.

chaosScenarios.name: Synchronous Bank Call Slowdown
chaosScenarios.description: Bank / card network latency rises from ~500ms to 5s while authorization runs inline on the request path
chaosScenarios.expectedBehavior: Payment-service threads block on the inline bank call; in-flight requests stack toward the 30s gateway timeout, instance connection pools fill, and new requests queue or 5xx. Client retries amplify the pile-up — the classic synchronous-coupling failure.
mitigationSteps: Enforce a 3s bank-call timeout — fail the request rather than hold connections
Shed load at the API gateway to keep the service inside its concurrency budget
Treat timed-out charges as UNKNOWN, not FAILED: re-query the bank by reference before permitting a retry
Structural fix: move bank calls behind a queue and worker pool so client latency decouples from acquirer health

chaosScenarios.name: Ledger Database Failure
chaosScenarios.description: The shared PostgreSQL ledger primary crashes
chaosScenarios.expectedBehavior: Both payment-service and notification-service lose their backing store: charges fail outright and webhook bookkeeping halts. Replica promotion takes 30-60s; any charge between bank approval and ledger commit is left in limbo.
mitigationSteps: Promote the replica and verify replication lag was zero
Re-drive limbo charges by querying the bank with the gateway reference (idempotent)
Replay queued events from Kafka — 30-day retention covers any realistic outage
Reconcile the ledger against bank records before resuming webhooks

chaosScenarios.name: Webhook Service Outage
chaosScenarios.description: The notification service crashes; merchant webhooks stop flowing
chaosScenarios.expectedBehavior: Charges keep processing, but merchants stop receiving confirmations while Kafka buffers events durably. Merchant systems that gate fulfillment on webhooks stall and support volume rises. On recovery, the backlog delivers as a burst — at-least-once, so merchants see duplicates.
mitigationSteps: Restart or scale notification instances; the consumer group resumes from committed offsets
Throttle the backlog drain so merchant endpoints are not flooded
Verify merchants deduplicate by event ID; signed payloads let them trust replays
Advise merchants to poll the charge API as a fallback during the outage

bottleneckProgression.description: Traffic approaches the contracted 500 RPS acquirer ceiling; authorizations queue or get throttled upstream
bottleneckProgression.resolution: Negotiate a higher rate tier or add a second acquirer with routing

bottleneckProgression.description: Each in-flight request holds a connection for the full ~500ms bank round trip; required concurrency grows linearly with RPS (Little’s law)
bottleneckProgression.resolution: Add instances, adopt non-blocking IO, or restructure to async queue-based processing

bottleneckProgression.description: payment-service and notification-service share the 200-connection ledger pool; webhook bookkeeping competes with money movement
bottleneckProgression.resolution: Add a connection pooler, split webhook delivery state into its own store, and scale read replicas

expectedIssues.title: Availability Coupled to the Bank
expectedIssues.description: The inline bank call means the acquirer 2% baseline error rate and tail latency surface directly as client-visible failures and slow requests
expectedIssues.mitigation: Strict timeouts and circuit breaking now; an async worker tier (return 202, process from the queue) as the structural fix

expectedIssues.title: Limbo Charges on Mid-Flight Crashes
expectedIssues.description: A crash after bank approval but before the ledger commit moves money with no record of it
expectedIssues.mitigation: Write a pre-authorization intent row before calling the bank; sweep intents without outcomes and re-query the bank by reference

expectedIssues.title: Duplicate Webhook Deliveries
expectedIssues.description: At-least-once consumption from Kafka plus delivery retries means merchants receive duplicate events
expectedIssues.mitigation: Stable event IDs, HMAC-signed payloads, documented merchant-side dedup, and exponential backoff per endpoint

expectedIssues.title: Shared Ledger Contention
expectedIssues.description: Webhook delivery-state writes share the ledger connection pool and IOPS with charge processing
expectedIssues.mitigation: Move delivery tracking to a separate schema or store and cap the notification-service pool share

steps: Confirm elevated latency on the acquirer status dashboard
Tighten the bank-call timeout and lower the gateway rate limit to protect concurrency headroom
Mark timed-out charges UNKNOWN and run the bank re-query sweeper
Restore rate limits gradually as bank latency recovers
Check consumer lag and notification-service health
Scale instances; drain the backlog throttled to protect merchant endpoints
Spot-check merchant dedup behavior on replayed events
Promote the replica and verify replication lag was zero
Sweep intent rows without outcomes; re-query the bank per reference
Reconcile ledger against bank records before re-enabling webhooks
Document limbo-charge resolution for the audit trail

decisions.title: Synchronous Authorization in the Request Path
decisions.context: Merchants want a single API call that returns the charge outcome immediately
decisions.decision: The Payment Service calls the bank inline (~500ms) and returns the terminal result in the response
consequences: Simplest possible merchant integration — no polling or completion webhooks needed for the happy path
Client-visible latency and availability inherit the bank tail behavior
Required concurrency scales with bank latency (Little’s law)

decisions.title: Async Webhooks via Kafka
decisions.context: Downstream notifications must not slow or fail the money path
decisions.decision: Charge outcomes publish to Kafka; a separate notification service delivers webhooks with retries

decisions.title: Relational Ledger as Source of Truth
decisions.context: Payment state must survive crashes and support reconciliation
decisions.decision: All charge state and accounting rows live in PostgreSQL with replicas
consequences: A single write primary is the scaling and availability choke point
Both services share one database, so contention must be managed

tradeoffs.benefit: One-call integration with an immediate answer
tradeoffs.cost: Bank brownouts directly degrade client latency and availability

tradeoffs.benefit: No confirmation is ever silently lost

tradeoffs.choice: Shared ledger DB for both services
tradeoffs.benefit: One database to operate, with transactional consistency across charge and delivery state
tradeoffs.cost: Webhook load can contend with charge processing

alternatives.name: Async Worker Processing (202 + Queue)
alternatives.description: Accept the charge, return 202, and process bank calls from a worker pool
alternatives.prosVsCons: Decouples client latency from the bank and absorbs brownouts, but merchants must handle asynchronous completion
alternatives.whyNotChosen: This design optimizes for integration simplicity; the async variant is the documented evolution path once volume or bank instability demands it

alternatives.name: Direct Webhook Calls (No Queue)
alternatives.description: The payment service calls merchant webhooks directly after charging
alternatives.prosVsCons: Fewer moving parts, but webhook failures would complicate the charge path and retry logic would live inside the money service
alternatives.whyNotChosen: Durable buffering and replay justify the queue

alternatives.name: Distributed / NoSQL Ledger
alternatives.description: Shard charge state across a NoSQL store for write scale
alternatives.prosVsCons: Higher write ceilings, but losing multi-row ACID transactions makes balanced accounting and reconciliation far harder
alternatives.whyNotChosen: Transactional integrity outweighs raw throughput at this scale
